 Fitness for Diabetics Pt I: Start exercising with confidence 
 by
 20261114182717 20261115 Keeon Tay­lor
 World Di­a­betes Day, ob­served on No­vem­ber 14, is a re­minder to pay at­ten­tion to a con­di­tion af­fect­ing many fam­i­lies in Trinidad and To­ba­go. But for some­one re­cent­ly told they have pre­di­a­betes or type 2 di­a­betes, that re­minder may al­ready be on their mind.
 You left the doc­tor’s of­fice promis­ing your­self you would take your health more se­ri­ous­ly. You planned to walk more, eat bet­ter and fi­nal­ly make time for ex­er­cise.
 But weeks have passed. Work still fills your day; you get home tired, and the walk you planned keeps get­ting pushed to to­mor­row. Mean­while, your next ap­point­ment is get­ting clos­er.
 The wor­ry is still there, along with frus­tra­tion that you have not fol­lowed through. Know­ing you need to make changes, how­ev­er, does not al­ways mean know­ing where to be­gin.
 The In­ter­na­tion­al Di­a­betes Fed­er­a­tion es­ti­mates that 151,200 adults aged 20 to 79 in Trinidad and To­ba­go were liv­ing with di­a­betes in 2024. Near­ly one in four adults with the con­di­tion were un­di­ag­nosed.
 These fig­ures show the im­por­tance of aware­ness and care. For those al­ready di­ag­nosed, prac­ti­cal sup­port mat­ters too.
 Start with some­thing 
 you can re­peat
 A de­mand­ing ex­er­cise pro­gramme may feel like the an­swer af­ter wor­ry­ing health news. Yet a rou­tine that leaves you over­whelmed can be dif­fi­cult to main­tain.
 The US Cen­tres for Dis­ease Con­trol and Pre­ven­tion ex­plains that phys­i­cal ac­tiv­i­ty helps peo­ple with di­a­betes man­age blood sug­ar. It rec­om­mends start­ing slow­ly, per­haps with a ten-minute walk af­ter din­ner, and grad­u­al­ly build­ing up.
 Choose a time that fits your day and put it in your cal­en­dar. “I will walk af­ter din­ner on Mon­day, Wednes­day and Fri­day” gives you a clear­er plan than “I need to ex­er­cise more.”
 If ten min­utes feels too much, start with five. As your fit­ness im­proves, grad­u­al­ly in­crease what you do. A short walk is a start­ing point, rather than the lim­it of your progress.
 If you miss a day, re­turn at the next op­por­tu­ni­ty. You do not have to wait un­til Mon­day to con­tin­ue.
 Build strength with 
 the right sup­port
 Walk­ing is use­ful, but strength ex­er­cis­es al­so de­serve at­ten­tion. The US Na­tion­al In­sti­tute of Di­a­betes and Di­ges­tive and Kid­ney Dis­eases rec­om­mends mus­cle-strength­en­ing ac­tiv­i­ties twice a week. These might in­clude wall push-ups or ex­er­cis­es with light weights or re­sis­tance bands.
 Learn to move with con­trol be­fore in­creas­ing the chal­lenge.
 If you have di­a­betes, dis­cuss suit­able ac­tiv­i­ties with your health­care team. Some di­a­betes med­i­cines can cause low blood sug­ar dur­ing or af­ter ex­er­cise, so ask what pre­cau­tions you need. Ex­er­cise sup­ports your care along­side food choic­es, check­ups and any pre­scribed treat­ment.
 For now, choose one man­age­able ac­tiv­i­ty and de­cide when you will do it.
 But what hap­pens when your first busy week ar­rives and that promise starts slip­ping again?
 In part two, we will look at how to ad­just your rou­tine when time, en­er­gy and mo­ti­va­tion run short.
 Keeon Tay­lor is a per­son­al train­er with over 14 years of ex­pe­ri­ence coach­ing women, fo­cus­ing on those aged 35 to 50. He works close­ly with women nav­i­gat­ing pre­menopause and oth­er life stages that bring big phys­i­cal changes.
